title: Applied Twice
statement: Let $\pi$ be a permutation of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$, chosen uniformly at random from all $12!$ permutations. For a subset $S$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$, write $\pi^2(S) = \{\pi(\pi(s)) : s \in S\}$. The probability that no nonempty subset $S$ with $|S| \le 3$ satisfies $\pi^2(S) = S$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m + n$.
hints: Take an element $s$ of a set $S$ with $\pi^2(S) = S$. Which other elements are forced into $S$? Work out what the smallest possible sets of this kind look like.

Use the cycle decomposition. A set with $\pi^2(S) = S$ is a union of cycles of $\pi^2$, so the condition says that every cycle of $\pi^2$ has length at least $4$. To see what squaring does to an $l$-cycle of $\pi$, model that cycle as the map $x \mapsto x + 1$ on the integers modulo $l$, so that $\pi^2$ acts as $x \mapsto x + 2$.

Under squaring, an odd $l$-cycle stays a single $l$-cycle, and an even $l$-cycle splits into two cycles of length $\frac{l}{2}$. So the cycles of $\pi$ must have odd length at least $5$ or even length at least $8$. The only ways to write $12$ as a sum of such lengths are $12$ and $7 + 5$. It remains to find the proportion of permutations with each of these two cycle types.
solution: First we restate the condition in terms of cycles. Suppose $\pi^2(S) = S$ and $s \in S$. Then $S$ contains $\pi^2(s)$, $\pi^4(s)$ and so on, which is the whole cycle of $\pi^2$ through $s$. So $S$ is a union of cycles of $\pi^2$. Conversely, the set of elements of any one cycle of $\pi^2$ is mapped onto itself by $\pi^2$. Hence a nonempty $S$ with $|S| \le 3$ and $\pi^2(S) = S$ exists exactly when $\pi^2$ has a cycle of length at most $3$. The required event is therefore that every cycle of $\pi^2$ has length at least $4$. Next we find how squaring acts on a cycle of $\pi$. Label an $l$-cycle of $\pi$ by the integers modulo $l$, so that $\pi$ acts as $x \mapsto x + 1$ and $\pi^2$ acts as $x \mapsto x + 2$. If $l$ is odd, then $2$ generates the integers modulo $l$, so the cycle stays a single cycle of length $l$. If $l$ is even, then the even and odd residues form two separate cycles, each of length $\frac{l}{2}$. So an odd $l$ is allowed exactly when $l \ge 5$, and an even $l$ is allowed exactly when $\frac{l}{2} \ge 4$, that is, $l \ge 8$. The allowed cycle lengths are $5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12$. The cycle lengths of $\pi$ must sum to $12$. Every length is at least $5$, so there are at most two cycles, since three would need at least $15$ elements. With one cycle, the length is $12$, which is allowed. With two cycles, the shorter has length $5$ or $6$, giving $5 + 7$ or $6 + 6$. The second of these is excluded because $6$ is not allowed. So $\pi$ is either a $12$-cycle or a product of a disjoint $7$-cycle and $5$-cycle. There are $11!$ cycles of length $12$, which is a proportion $\frac{11!}{12!} = \frac{1}{12}$ of all permutations. For the other type, choose the $5$ elements of the $5$-cycle, then arrange each cycle, giving $$\binom{12}{5} \cdot 4! \cdot 6! = \dfrac{12!}{5! \cdot 7!} \cdot 4! \cdot 6! = \dfrac{12!}{5 \cdot 7}$$ permutations, a proportion $\frac{1}{35}$. The two types are disjoint, so the probability is $$\dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{35} = \dfrac{47}{420}.$$ Since $47$ is prime and does not divide $420$, this fraction is in lowest terms. So $m = 47$ and $n = 420$, and the answer is $m + n = 467$. Why this works. cycle-decomposition, favorable-over-total: sets fixed by $\pi^2$ are unions of its cycles, so the condition restricts the cycle type of $\pi$ to two cases whose proportions are easy to count.
